rationale:
Evidence: iteration 5 (score 521.7) is still the best design. Seven sensors at x = -0.075 to +0.075 m, y = 0.07 m, sensor size 0.016 m, kp 5.0, kd 0.6, ki 0, base_speed 1.1. It finishes the oval 20/20 at about 1.99 s. Its s-bend progress is 0.78 and its slalom progress is 0.40. All failures are off_track with max_error 0.059 to 0.064 m, just past the fixed 0.06 m limit. Steering oscillation is moderate (0.24 to 0.43), so the robot lags on bends rather than jittering.

What the later iterations established. Iteration 6 (wider, forward array) hurt. Iteration 7 (base_speed 1.0) hurt, so slower is not safer. Iteration 8 (base_speed 1.2) scored 501, slightly below iteration 5, so the speed optimum sits near 1.1. Gain increases in iterations 3 and 4 hurt the oval, though those runs also changed other variables.

Change (one variable, geometry only): mass 0.5 -> 0.4 kg, the lower bound. Yaw inertia scales with mass, so a lighter robot should turn faster in response to the same wheel-speed difference. That should reduce the lag on bends that produces max_error just above 0.06 m. Sensors, gains, speed and line_loss stay as in iteration 5, so any change in s-bend and slalom progress can be attributed to mass. Earlier mass drops (0.6 to 0.5, iteration 2) came with other changes, so this isolates its effect.

Expected result: s-bend progress rises to 0.85 or more with more finishes than 5/20. Slalom progress rises toward 0.45. The oval stays near 20/20 with completion_time about 2.0 s. Steering oscillation should stay below about 0.45.

Hypotheses: H1, lower yaw inertia reduces bend lag and max_error. H2, the oval finish rate holds because the controller gains are unchanged. H3, if max_error does not fall, the limit is sensing range or gain balance rather than inertia, and the next step should test kd between 0.6 and 0.8.

Next measurements: completion and progress per track, max_error and rms_error (is the lag reduced), steering_oscillation (is the response too fast), line_loss_events, and completion_time.
